headline: Marine Parkway at midnight: the bass are there, you just gotta wait for dark
subhead: Daytime's dead in the bay, but the bridge and the inlet blues are keeping this a two-tide, two-species week worth working around.
body_markdown:
I took the kayak out of the launch at Sunset Cove Tuesday morning because I figured I'd beat the heat and the boat traffic both. Wrong on the heat, right on the traffic — I had the flats mostly to myself by 6 a.m., which tells you something about where everybody else's head is at right now. Nobody wants to paddle in July soup unless they know something's biting, and honestly, that's fair. It's been a quiet week on the daytime program.

Here's the honest version: the bay has slid into that classic late-July pattern where the stripers just don't want to play during daylight. Water's sitting warm and stable, no wind to speak of, and that combination pushes bass off the flats and onto the thermocline or tight against deep structure where it's cooler. I marked fish on the sounder over by the Cross Bay Bridge pilings in about 14 feet and couldn't get so much as a look during the mid-morning hours. That's not bad luck, that's just where we are in the calendar.

So I've shifted my whole week to the night program, and if you want fish right now, you should too. Marine Parkway Bridge on the last two hours of the outgoing has been the most consistent thing I've fished all month. I've been running there by boat right at dusk, anchoring up-current of the pilings on the Rockaway side and drifting bucktails — half-ounce white with a strip of fresh bunker on the hook for scent — right down into the shadow line. The bass are stacking on that current edge waiting for whatever gets swept through, and they'll hold there most of the night once the tide gets moving good. Had three keepers in the 26 to 29-inch range last Thursday night working that exact drift, all right in that first hour of hard outgoing water. After the tide goes slack, it shuts off fast, so don't waste your whole night there — get in position, fish the push, then move.

For shore guys who can't get out at midnight, Breezy Point after dark is your play. Swimmers — I like a 6-inch Redfin in bone or bunker pattern — worked slow along the surf line where the beach drops into that first trough. You're fishing the edge where the bay water meeting the ocean creates just enough temperature break to hold bait, and the bass know it. It's not a numbers game out there right now, more like two or three solid fish a night if you put in the time and fish the two hours around the tide change.

Now the blues — this is the one story in the whole zone that doesn't require patience or darkness. We flagged this pattern building last week, said the bunker-driven blitz would keep spreading as long as the bait stayed put and the weather held calm, and that's exactly what's happening. Rockaway Inlet has had bluefish on bunker schools nearly every morning this week, visible from the beach at Beach 9th and Beach 90th, birds working right over the bait balls. If you can get out in a boat or even paddle the kayak out toward the inlet mouth, casting into those boils with a metal — I've been throwing a 2-ounce Hopkins in chrome — is about as close to guaranteed as this bay gets right now. Just watch your leader, these blues are chopping through 20-pound fluoro like it's nothing. I've gone to 40-pound mono leader just to stop losing lures every third cast.

Fluke fishing is the disappointment of the week, if I'm being straight with you. The flats between Ruffle Bar and Big Egg Marsh are still holding fish, but it's short after short after short. If you want a keeper, you need to get onto the deeper channel edges — I'm talking 18 to 22 feet along the edges of the Cross Bay Bridge channel — and slow-drift white Gulp Swimming Mullets on a 3/4-ounce bucktail right on bottom. That's where the bigger fish are hiding out from the heat. Don't waste your morning on the shallow grass flats unless you're fine with a bucket of shorts and no dinner.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. No real wind in the forecast, water's stable and warm, so I'd keep planning around the tides rather than the clock — fish the last two hours of any outgoing after sundown for bass, and hit the inlet at first light for blues while the bunker are still balled up tight. If a front comes through and stirs things up, that could actually help the daytime bass bite by mixing some cooler water back into the upper bay, but until that happens, I'm sticking with my night rod and my early alarm for the blues. Canarsie Pier folks, don't sleep on the blues either — they've been showing up along that stretch too when the tide's right, so it's worth a look even without a boat.
